memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.intro: On 24 April Armenians around the world remember the victims of the 1915 genocide in the Ottoman Empire, in which an estimated 1.5 million Armenians lost their lives.
memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.history: On 24 April 1915 hundreds of Armenian intellectuals and community leaders were arrested in Constantinople, the event that came to mark the beginning of the deportations and massacres. Armenia has observed the day officially since 1988, and it became a public holiday after independence.
memorial_am_armenian_genocide_remembranc.traditions: Hundreds of thousands walk up to the Tsitsernakaberd memorial in Yerevan to lay flowers around the eternal flame. Church services, a minute of silence and concerts of remembrance take place across Armenia and the diaspora.
funFacts: The Tsitsernakaberd memorial was opened in 1967; its twelve basalt slabs symbolise the lost provinces of historic Western Armenia.
The forget-me-not became the official symbol of the centenary in 2015 and is still worn today.
More than 30 countries have formally recognised the events of 1915 as genocide.

memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.intro: 24 March, the Day of Remembrance for Truth and Justice, marks the anniversary of the 1976 military coup in Argentina and honours the victims of the dictatorship that followed.
memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.history: On 24 March 1976 the armed forces overthrew President Isabel Perón and ruled until 1983. During those years an estimated 30,000 people were kidnapped, tortured and 'disappeared'. The day was created by law in 2002 and became a public holiday in 2006.
memorial_ar_day_of_remembrance_for_truth.traditions: Human-rights organisations, above all the Mothers and Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo, lead a large march to the Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires. Schools hold lessons on memory and democracy, and former detention centres such as the ESMA open their doors.
funFacts: The white headscarf of the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo, originally a cloth nappy, became the symbol of the search for the disappeared.
The Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo have identified more than 130 grandchildren born in captivity.
'Nunca más' (Never again) is the title of the 1984 report of the truth commission and the motto of the day.

memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.intro: On 2 April Argentina remembers the soldiers who fought and fell in the 1982 war over the Malvinas (Falkland Islands) and honours the veterans.
memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.history: On 2 April 1982 Argentine forces landed on the islands, whose sovereignty Argentina has claimed since 1833. The 74-day war with the United Kingdom cost 649 Argentine and 255 British lives. The day was established in 2000 and became a public holiday in 2001.
memorial_ar_day_of_the_veterans_and_fall.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Monument to the Fallen in Malvinas on Plaza San Martín in Buenos Aires and in towns across the country. Veterans parade, flags fly at half mast in the morning, and schools recall the islands' history.
funFacts: The monument on Plaza San Martín lists the names of all 649 Argentine fallen on black marble slabs.
Many of the conscripts were only 18 or 19 years old.
The Darwin cemetery on the islands holds the graves of 237 Argentine soldiers; families have been able to visit since 1991.

memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.intro: Argentina commemorates the death of General José de San Martín, the liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru, who died on 17 August 1850 in France.
memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.history: San Martín led the Army of the Andes across the mountains in 1817, helped free Chile and proclaimed the independence of Peru in 1821. He spent his final decades in exile in Europe. The holiday was created in 1938 and is moved to a Monday to form a long weekend.
memorial_ar_general_jose_de_san_martin_m.traditions: Wreaths are laid at his mausoleum in the Metropolitan Cathedral of Buenos Aires, guarded by the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers he founded. Schools stage plays and sing the 'March of San Lorenzo'.
funFacts: San Martín is known as the 'Father of the Nation' and appears on many Argentine banknotes and coins.
His remains were brought back from France to Buenos Aires in 1880.
The crossing of the Andes covered passes higher than 4,000 metres with about 5,000 soldiers.

memorial_ar_general_manuel_belgrano_memo.intro: Argentina marks 20 June in memory of General Manuel Belgrano, who died on that date in 1820. Known as the Day of the Flag, it honours the lawyer, economist and military leader who created the Argentine flag and is counted among the country's founding figures.
memorial_ar_general_manuel_belgrano_memo.history: Belgrano was born in Buenos Aires in 1770 and took a leading part in the May Revolution of 1810 and the wars of independence that followed. On 27 February 1812, on the banks of the Paraná at Rosario, he raised a light blue and white flag for the first time; it became the national flag. He died in Buenos Aires on 20 June 1820, impoverished and in the middle of civil conflict. Law 12,361, passed in 1938, made 20 June the annual observance in his memory.
memorial_ar_general_manuel_belgrano_memo.traditions: The central ceremony takes place at the National Flag Memorial in Rosario, where the flag was first raised. The president usually attends, and military units, veterans of the Malvinas conflict, police and civic organisations take part in a parade. Wreaths are laid at Belgrano's tomb in Buenos Aires, and fourth-grade pupils across the country traditionally make their promise of loyalty to the flag around this date.
funFacts: Belgrano first raised the light blue and white flag at Rosario on 27 February 1812.
The observance follows the date of his death in 1820, not the date the flag was created.
Argentine fourth-graders traditionally make their promise of loyalty to the flag on this day.

memorial_at_day_of_remembrance_against_v.intro: Austria's Day of Remembrance against Violence and Racism in Memory of the Victims of National Socialism falls on 5 May. It commemorates those persecuted and killed under Nazi rule and marks the liberation of the Mauthausen concentration camp in 1945.
memorial_at_day_of_remembrance_against_v.history: United States troops reached the Mauthausen concentration camp in Upper Austria on 5 May 1945, days before the end of the war in Europe. The Austrian National Council resolved unanimously on 11 November 1997 that the date should be observed each year as a day of remembrance against violence and racism, and it was first held in 1998. Austria chose its own date rather than 27 January, the day marked in Germany and by the United Nations, reflecting a shift away from the post-war view of the country solely as a victim of Nazi Germany.
memorial_at_day_of_remembrance_against_v.traditions: Parliament holds a special commemorative session in the National Council chamber, usually with an address by a survivor or a historian, and flags on public buildings are flown at half-mast. The Mauthausen Memorial hosts an international liberation ceremony on the first Sunday after 5 May, with delegations from many countries, wreath-laying and a roll call of remembrance. Schools and cultural institutions arrange projects and readings.
funFacts: The National Council adopted the day unanimously on 11 November 1997, and it was first observed in 1998.
The date marks the liberation of the Mauthausen concentration camp by United States forces on 5 May 1945.
The Mauthausen Memorial holds its international liberation ceremony on the first Sunday after 5 May.

memorial_au_anzac_day.intro: Anzac Day on 25 April honours Australians and New Zealanders who served and died in wars, marking the 1915 Gallipoli landing.
memorial_au_anzac_day.history: On 25 April 1915 the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) landed at Gallipoli in Ottoman Turkey during the First World War. The costly campaign became a defining national memory, and the date now commemorates all who served.
memorial_au_anzac_day.traditions: The day begins with solemn dawn services, followed by marches of veterans, the playing of the Last Post and the words "Lest we forget". People wear rosemary sprigs and play two-up, a traditional coin game.
funFacts: ANZAC stands for Australian and New Zealand Army Corps.
Dawn services recall the early-morning Gallipoli landing.
Two-up is an Anzac Day tradition. The conditions under which it is permitted depend on state rules.

memorial_ba_srebrenica_remembrance_day.intro: Srebrenica Genocide Remembrance Day is marked on 11 July in Bosnia and Herzegovina and, since 2024, internationally. It remembers the Bosniak men and boys killed at Srebrenica in July 1995, the worst atrocity in Europe since the Second World War.
memorial_ba_srebrenica_remembrance_day.history: In July 1995 Bosnian Serb forces under Ratko Mladic took the United Nations declared safe area of Srebrenica. Thousands of Bosniak civilians fled to the UN base at Potocari, and in the days that followed at least 8,372 men and boys were killed and buried in mass graves, many of which were later disturbed to conceal the crime. International courts have ruled the killings a genocide. The Srebrenica-Potocari Memorial and Cemetery opened on 20 September 2003, and in May 2024 the UN General Assembly designated 11 July an international day of reflection and commemoration.
memorial_ba_srebrenica_remembrance_day.traditions: The central commemoration takes place at Potocari, where victims identified during the past year through DNA analysis are buried together in a collective funeral attended by tens of thousands of mourners and foreign delegations. Their names are read aloud, prayers are said and green-draped coffins are carried through the crowd to the graves. In the days beforehand the Peace March, Mars mira, retraces in reverse the forest route taken by those who fled in 1995.
funFacts: The memorial and cemetery at Potocari opened on 20 September 2003, on the site of the former United Nations base.
The UN General Assembly designated 11 July an international day of reflection and commemoration in May 2024.
The Peace March retraces over several days the forest route taken by those who fled Srebrenica in July 1995.

memorial_bd_language_martyrs_day.intro: Language Martyrs' Day, Shohid Dibosh, is observed in Bangladesh on 21 February. It remembers the students and others shot dead in Dhaka in 1952 while demanding that Bengali be recognised as a state language of Pakistan.
memorial_bd_language_martyrs_day.history: After the partition of 1947 the government of Pakistan moved to make Urdu the sole state language, although Bengali speakers formed the largest language group in the country. On 21 February 1952 students defied a ban on gatherings at the University of Dhaka, and police opened fire near the East Bengal Legislative Assembly, killing demonstrators including Abdus Salam, Rafiq Uddin Ahmed, Abul Barkat and Abdul Jabbar. Strikes and protests followed across the province. After the United Front formed a provincial government in 1954, the anniversary was declared a holiday.
memorial_bd_language_martyrs_day.traditions: Observance begins at midnight with wreath-laying at the Shaheed Minar in Dhaka, the monument raised at the site of the shootings, and at its replicas across the country. Mourners often walk barefoot in slow processions carrying flowers, the national flag flies at half-mast on public buildings, and the mourning song Amar Bhaier Rokte Rangano is sung. Readings, exhibitions and book fairs accompany the day.
funFacts: UNESCO proclaimed 21 February International Mother Language Day in 1999, giving the anniversary worldwide recognition.
The Shaheed Minar in Dhaka stands near the place where demonstrators were shot in February 1952.
The anniversary was first declared a holiday after the United Front formed a provincial government in 1954.

memorial_bd_victory_day.intro: Victory Day, Bijoy Dibosh, is Bangladesh's national holiday on 16 December. It marks the surrender of Pakistani forces in Dhaka in 1971, which ended the Bangladesh Liberation War and secured the country's independence.
memorial_bd_victory_day.history: The war began in March 1971, after the Pakistani army moved against the independence movement in what was then East Pakistan. Months of fighting by the Mukti Bahini, joined in December by Indian forces, ended on 16 December 1971, when Lieutenant General A. A. K. Niazi signed the Instrument of Surrender at the Ramna Race Course in Dhaka. It was accepted by Lieutenant General Jagjit Singh Aurora, joint commander of the Indian and Bangladesh forces. The date has been observed as Victory Day since 1972.
memorial_bd_victory_day.traditions: The day opens with a gun salute at dawn. The head of state and other leaders lay wreaths at the National Martyrs' Memorial at Savar, outside Dhaka, which then receives crowds of visitors all day. A parade is held at the National Parade Ground, flags are raised on homes and public buildings, and buildings are lit in the national red and green. Prayers and memorial services are held for those killed in 1971.
funFacts: India marks the same date as Vijay Diwas, recalling its part in the 1971 war.
The National Martyrs' Memorial at Savar is the focus of the national wreath-laying.
Victory Day has been observed since 1972, the first year after independence.

memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.intro: The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on 30 September honours the children who were sent to residential schools and the survivors, families and communities affected. It has been a federal holiday since 2021.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.history: For more than a century about 150,000 Indigenous children were taken to church-run residential schools, where many suffered abuse and thousands died. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission called for a day of remembrance in 2015, and Parliament created the holiday in 2021 after indications of possible unmarked burials were reported in Kamloops.
memorial_ca_national_day_for_truth_and_r.traditions: Canadians wear orange shirts, a custom started by survivor Phyllis Webstad, whose new orange shirt was taken from her on her first day at school. Communities hold walks, ceremonies and moments of silence, and buildings are lit in orange.
funFacts: The date was chosen because children were taken from their families in late September.
Orange Shirt Day began in Williams Lake, British Columbia, in 2013.
The message of the day is "Every Child Matters".
The last residential school closed in 1996.

memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.intro: On 2 August the Democratic Republic of the Congo commemorates the victims of the wars and mass atrocities in the east of the country since 1996, a day known as 'Genocost'.
memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.history: The date recalls the outbreak of the Second Congo War on 2 August 1998, in which several African states and countless armed groups were involved. The conflicts in the east have claimed millions of lives through violence, hunger and disease. The government made 2 August a national day of remembrance in 2022.
memorial_cd_congolese_genocide_day.traditions: A national ceremony is held in Kisangani, a city that suffered heavy fighting in 2000, with a minute of silence at midday. Churches hold services, and civil-society groups organise marches and exhibitions.
funFacts: The word 'Genocost' combines 'genocide' and 'cost' to point to the economic motives behind the violence.
The Second Congo War is sometimes called 'Africa's World War' because nine countries took part.
Nobel Peace Prize laureate Denis Mukwege, a doctor from Bukavu, has long campaigned for the recognition of the victims.

memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.intro: On 16 January the Democratic Republic of the Congo remembers President Laurent-Désiré Kabila, who was assassinated in Kinshasa in 2001.
memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.history: Kabila led the rebellion that ended Mobutu Sese Seko's rule in 1997 and became president. On 16 January 2001 he was shot by one of his bodyguards in the presidential palace. His son Joseph Kabila succeeded him and led the country to the 2002 peace agreement.
memorial_cd_laurent_desire_kabila_assass.traditions: Official ceremonies are held at Kabila's mausoleum in front of the Palais de la Nation in Kinshasa, where wreaths are laid. The day is a public holiday and is often marked together with the Lumumba commemoration on the following day.
funFacts: Kabila is honoured with the title 'Mzee', a Swahili word of respect for an elder.
His mausoleum in Kinshasa was inaugurated in 2002 and features a bronze statue.
16 and 17 January together form two consecutive days of remembrance for the country's two 'heroes of independence'.

memorial_cd_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day, known in the Democratic Republic of the Congo as the day of the martyrs of independence, falls on 4 January. It remembers those who died in Léopoldville, today's Kinshasa, at the start of the country's independence movement.
memorial_cd_martyrs_day.history: On 4 January 1959 a crowd gathered in Léopoldville for a meeting of the Alliance des Bakongo, ABAKO. When the colonial authorities refused to allow the gathering, unrest spread through the city and was suppressed harshly; the number of dead is disputed and has never been established with certainty. The events pushed Belgium to convene a round table conference in Brussels, and the Congo became independent on 30 June 1960. Congolese have marked the date since the 1960s as la journée des martyrs de l’indépendance.
memorial_cd_martyrs_day.traditions: The day is a public holiday. Official ceremonies include the laying of wreaths on graves and memorials, addresses by public officials and religious services for the dead. Radio and television carry programmes on the independence movement, and civic and political groups use the occasion to recall those who died in 1959 and in the struggles that followed.
funFacts: The events of 4 January 1959 are widely seen as a turning point on the road to Congolese independence.
Independence followed less than eighteen months later, on 30 June 1960.
Léopoldville, where the events took place, was renamed Kinshasa in 1966.

memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.intro: 17 January commemorates Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the independent Congo, who was murdered in 1961.
memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.history: Lumumba led the Congo to independence from Belgium on 30 June 1960 but was overthrown within months during the Congo Crisis. He was handed over to secessionist forces in Katanga and executed on 17 January 1961 with Belgian complicity, as a Belgian parliamentary inquiry acknowledged in 2001.
memorial_cd_patrice_lumumba_assassinatio.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Lumumba monument on the Boulevard Lumumba in Kinshasa and in his home region. His independence speech is read in schools, and the day is a public holiday.
funFacts: Lumumba was only 35 years old when he was killed.
In 2022 Belgium returned a gold-capped tooth, the only remaining relic of his body, to his family; it was buried in a mausoleum in Kinshasa.
He is regarded as one of the leading figures of African independence movements and appears on the country's banknotes.

memorial_cn_nanjing_massacre_memorial_da.intro: National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims is observed in China on 13 December. It remembers the civilians and disarmed soldiers killed after Japanese forces captured Nanjing in 1937, together with Chinese victims of the wider war.
memorial_cn_nanjing_massacre_memorial_da.history: Japanese troops entered Nanjing, then the capital of China, on 13 December 1937. Over the following weeks the city was the scene of mass killings, sexual violence, looting and arson; Chinese accounts put the number of dead at about three hundred thousand, while estimates made elsewhere differ. A memorial hall was established in 1985 at Jiangdongmen in Nanjing, beside a wartime mass burial site. In 2014 the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress made 13 December a national memorial day, first observed in December of that year.
memorial_cn_nanjing_massacre_memorial_da.traditions: The state ceremony is held at the Memorial Hall of the Victims in Nanjing Massacre by Japanese Invaders, attended by senior officials, survivors and their descendants. The national flag is lowered to half-mast, a peace bell is rung and a minute of silence is kept while air-raid sirens sound across the city; traffic halts and pedestrians stand still. Wreaths are laid and doves are released at the close.
funFacts: The memorial hall at Jiangdongmen in Nanjing was established in 1985, next to a wartime mass burial site.
The national memorial day was created in 2014 by the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress.
Sirens sound across Nanjing during the ceremony and the whole city pauses for a minute of silence.

memorial_de_june_17_uprising.intro: 17 June commemorates the popular uprising of 1953 in East Germany, when more than a million people protested against the SED regime and were crushed by Soviet tanks.
memorial_de_june_17_uprising.history: The uprising began on 16 June 1953 with a strike by construction workers in East Berlin against increased work quotas and spread to hundreds of towns. Soviet troops violently suppressed the protests. In August 1953 West Germany established 17 June as the Day of German Unity; it was observed annually until reunification in 1990.
memorial_de_june_17_uprising.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the memorial in front of the former House of Ministries on Leipziger Straße in Berlin and at the graves of the victims in Seestraße cemetery. The Bundestag and state parliaments hold commemorations.
funFacts: The boulevard leading to the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin has been called 'Straße des 17. Juni' since 1953.
Around 15,000 people were arrested after the uprising.
The events are considered the first popular uprising against a communist regime in the Eastern Bloc.

memorial_de_november_pogroms.intro: 9 November commemorates the November pogroms of 1938, when synagogues, Jewish shops and homes across Germany and Austria were attacked and destroyed.
memorial_de_november_pogroms.history: In November 1938 the Nazi regime organised widespread violence against Jews. More than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms were destroyed, Jewish shops and homes were attacked, and about 30,000 Jewish men were imprisoned in concentration camps. The pogroms were a major escalation of Nazi persecution.
memorial_de_november_pogroms.traditions: Commemorations are held at synagogues and memorial sites; in many towns people clean the Stolpersteine, small brass plaques set into the pavement in front of the last homes of victims, and place candles beside them. Schools discuss the history of the day.
funFacts: 9 November is called Germany's 'day of fate': the republic was proclaimed in 1918 and the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 on the same date.
More than 100,000 Stolpersteine have been laid across Europe since 1992.
The term 'Kristallnacht' is often criticised for trivialising the violence; 'November pogroms' describes the persecution more clearly.

memorial_de_victims_of_national_socialis.intro: 27 January is Germany's day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism, the anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz concentration and extermination camp in 1945.
memorial_de_victims_of_national_socialis.history: Federal President Roman Herzog proclaimed the day in 1996. In 2005 the United Nations adopted 27 January as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Soviet troops liberated Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, where more than one million people had been murdered.
memorial_de_victims_of_national_socialis.traditions: The Bundestag holds a memorial hour with a speech by a survivor or a prominent guest. Flags fly at half mast on public buildings, and memorial sites, schools and churches organise events. Many people light a candle in their window in the evening.
funFacts: The day remembers all groups persecuted by the Nazis: Jews, Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities, homosexuals, political prisoners and many others.
The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin consists of 2,711 concrete stelae.
The words 'Never again' are the message that unites commemorations on this day worldwide.

memorial_de_volkstrauertag.intro: Volkstrauertag, Germany's national day of mourning, falls on the Sunday two weeks before the first Sunday of Advent, in mid-November. It remembers the dead of war and armed conflict of all nations, and the victims of violent oppression.
memorial_de_volkstrauertag.history: The German war graves commission, founded in 1919, proposed a day of remembrance for the fallen of the First World War, and it was first observed in 1922. Under National Socialism it was recast in 1934 as Heldengedenktag, a day of heroes, and moved to March. West Germany revived the earlier form of the observance in 1948, and in 1952 fixed it in late autumn, deliberately setting it apart from the Nazi-era version and widening its scope to include civilians and those killed under tyranny.
memorial_de_volkstrauertag.traditions: The central ceremony takes place in the Bundestag, where the Federal President gives an address in the presence of the chancellor, the cabinet and the diplomatic corps, followed by the national anthem and the lament Der gute Kamerad. Flags on public buildings fly at half-mast. Towns and parishes hold services and lay wreaths at war memorials and war graves, often with brass bands, choirs and volunteer fire brigades taking part.
funFacts: Volkstrauertag has no fixed date; it falls two Sundays before Advent, between 13 and 19 November.
It has been observed in its present late-autumn form since 1952.
In most German states it is a quiet day, when public dancing and loud events are restricted.

memorial_ee_victory_day.intro: Victory Day, or Võidupüha, is a public holiday in Estonia held on 23 June. It marks the victory of Estonian and Latvian forces in the Battle of Cēsis in 1919, a turning point in the Estonian War of Independence.
memorial_ee_victory_day.history: After declaring independence in 1918, Estonia fought the War of Independence against Soviet Russia and, in June 1919, against the Baltische Landeswehr in northern Latvia. Estonian troops, supported by Latvian units, prevailed at the Battle of Cēsis, known in Estonian as the Battle of Võnnu, on 23 June 1919. The Riigikogu declared the date a national holiday on 16 February 1934. Observance was banned under the German and Soviet occupations, and the holiday was restored in 1992 after Estonia regained independence.
memorial_ee_victory_day.traditions: The president hosts a military parade that rotates between Estonian cities and presents decorations to soldiers and volunteers. On the morning of the day the president lights a victory fire, and the flame is carried by relay across the country to kindle bonfires in towns and villages. Flags stay out through the night into St John's Day on 24 June, when families gather at midsummer fires.
funFacts: The battle is known in Estonian as the Battle of Võnnu, Võnnu being the Estonian name for the Latvian town of Cēsis.
The victory fire lit by the president is relayed across Estonia to light local bonfires the same evening.
Victory Day falls directly before St John's Day, giving Estonia two public holidays in a row at midsummer.

memorial_eu_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.intro: The European Day of Remembrance of Victims of Terrorism is observed across the European Union on 11 March. It honours everyone killed or injured by terrorism, whether the attacks took place inside Europe or beyond its borders.
memorial_eu_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.history: The date recalls the coordinated bombings of commuter trains in Madrid on 11 March 2004, in which 193 people were killed and around two thousand were injured. Shortly afterwards European leaders designated 11 March as an annual day of remembrance, first observed in 2005. Since then the European institutions and the member states have used the day to remember victims of terrorism worldwide, to give a voice to survivors and bereaved families, and to reaffirm support for them.
memorial_eu_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.traditions: European institutions in Brussels, Strasbourg and Luxembourg keep a minute of silence and fly flags at half-mast, and the European Commission holds a remembrance event at which victims and survivors speak. National governments hold their own ceremonies, and in Spain wreaths are laid at memorials in Madrid, including the monument at Atocha station. Victims' associations organise gatherings, readings of names and concerts.
funFacts: The day was created after the Madrid train bombings of 11 March 2004 and was first observed in 2005.
It remembers victims of terrorist attacks worldwide, not only those that happened within the European Union.
A memorial to the victims of the Madrid attacks stands at Atocha station in the centre of the city.

memorial_fr_armistice_day.intro: 11 November commemorates the 1918 armistice that ended the fighting on the Western Front and honours those who died for France.
memorial_fr_armistice_day.history: At 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918 the armistice signed at Compiègne silenced the guns of the Western Front. France lost some 1.4 million soldiers. Since 1922 the date has been a national day of remembrance, later extended to the fallen of all wars.
memorial_fr_armistice_day.traditions: The President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier beneath the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, where an eternal flame burns. Across the country, citizens and veterans gather at war memorials for a minute of silence.
funFacts: The armistice took effect at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month.
The eternal flame under the Arc de Triomphe is rekindled every evening since 1923.
The blue cornflower (le Bleuet) is France’s symbol of remembrance.

memorial_gb_remembrance_sunday.intro: Remembrance Sunday is observed in the United Kingdom on the second Sunday in November, the Sunday nearest to Armistice Day on 11 November. It honours the service members and civilians of Britain and the Commonwealth who died in the two world wars and in later conflicts.
memorial_gb_remembrance_sunday.history: The first national commemoration was held on 11 November 1919, a year after the armistice that ended the fighting of the First World War, with a two-minute silence observed across the country. After the Second World War the government decided that a Sunday observance would allow wider participation, and in 1946 Prime Minister Clement Attlee announced that the second Sunday in November would be known as Remembrance Sunday, in commemoration of both world wars. The dead of later conflicts were gradually included in the same act of remembrance.
memorial_gb_remembrance_sunday.traditions: The national service takes place at the Cenotaph in Whitehall, London, where the silence begins at eleven o'clock, marked by a gun and the Last Post. The monarch lays the first wreath of poppies, followed by members of the royal family, political leaders, Commonwealth representatives and the armed services, and veterans march past afterwards. Similar services are held at war memorials, churches and schools throughout the country.
funFacts: The two-minute silence at eleven o'clock recalls the hour the guns fell silent on 11 November 1918.
Paper poppies are sold each autumn by the Royal British Legion to support serving and former service personnel.
The Cenotaph in Whitehall, designed by Edwin Lutyens, was unveiled in its permanent stone form in 1920.

memorial_gi_workers_memorial_day.intro: Workers' Memorial Day on 28 April remembers people who have been killed, injured or made ill by their work. In Gibraltar it is a public holiday.
memorial_gi_workers_memorial_day.history: The day was started by Canadian trade unions in 1984 and is now observed in more than 100 countries. The International Labour Organization made 28 April the World Day for Safety and Health at Work in 2003. Gibraltar added it to its public holidays in 2009 at the initiative of the unions.
memorial_gi_workers_memorial_day.traditions: A wreath-laying ceremony takes place in Gibraltar, and unions hold a minute of silence for workers who lost their lives. The motto of the day is 'Remember the dead, fight for the living'.
funFacts: The date recalls 28 April 1914, when Ontario passed its first workers' compensation act.
Gibraltar is one of only a few places where the day is a full public holiday.
Purple ribbons and purple forget-me-nots are the symbols of the day in the United Kingdom.

memorial_hr_remembrance_day.intro: On 18 November Croatia remembers the victims of the Homeland War, above all the fall of Vukovar in 1991 and the massacre in Škabrnja on the same day.
memorial_hr_remembrance_day.history: After an 87-day siege the town of Vukovar fell to the Yugoslav People's Army and Serb paramilitaries on 18 November 1991. Around 200 wounded and staff were taken from the hospital and killed at the Ovčara farm. The day of remembrance was created in 1999 and became a public holiday in 2020.
memorial_hr_remembrance_day.traditions: Tens of thousands walk in the 'Column of Remembrance' from the Vukovar hospital to the memorial cemetery, where a candle is lit for every victim. Church bells ring across Croatia, and the water tower of Vukovar, riddled with bullet holes, has become the symbol of the town.
funFacts: The Vukovar water tower was hit more than 600 times during the siege and was opened as a memorial in 2020.
The memorial cemetery contains 938 white crosses, one for each of the identified victims from the mass graves.
The Croatian parliament made 18 November a public holiday in 2019, effective from 2020.

memorial_hu_1848_revolution_memorial_day.intro: Hungary's national holiday on 15 March recalls the revolution that began in Pest in 1848, when demonstrators demanded freedom of the press, civil rights and self-government within the Habsburg Empire.
memorial_hu_1848_revolution_memorial_day.history: On 15 March 1848 young radicals gathered at the Pilvax coffee house in Pest and set out through the city. The poet Sándor Petőfi recited his National Song, and the crowd took over the Landerer printing press to publish the Twelve Points, a list of demands that included freedom of the press, a responsible ministry in Buda-Pest, annual parliaments, equal taxation and the abolition of serfdom. The day passed without bloodshed, the political prisoner Mihály Táncsics was released, and Lajos Batthyány soon became prime minister. The date was restored as a public holiday in 1989.
memorial_hu_1848_revolution_memorial_day.traditions: People wear a cockade in the national red, white and green, pinned close to the heart. The day begins with a flag-raising ceremony in front of Parliament on Kossuth Square, followed by a hussar procession to the Hungarian National Museum, where speeches and recitals recall the events of 1848. Many museums open free of charge, and towns across the country hold their own ceremonies.
funFacts: The Twelve Points opened with the demand for freedom of the press and an end to censorship.
Petőfi's National Song was first recited in public on 15 March 1848 and is still read at ceremonies.
15 March is one of Hungary's three national holidays, alongside 20 August and 23 October.

memorial_hu_1956_revolution_memorial_day.intro: 1956 Revolution Memorial Day is one of Hungary's national holidays, observed every 23 October. It remembers the Hungarian Revolution of 1956, the uprising against Soviet domination that began in Budapest on that date, and all those who died when it was put down.
memorial_hu_1956_revolution_memorial_day.history: The revolution began on 23 October 1956, when university students in Budapest marched to demand reform and free elections; security forces opened fire on demonstrators outside the Hungarian Radio building. A new government under Imre Nagy briefly took office, but Soviet forces intervened and suppressed the uprising by 4 November, with fighting continuing in places until mid-November. Thousands of Hungarians died and around 200,000 left the country. Public commemoration was forbidden under communist rule. On 23 October 1989 the Third Hungarian Republic was proclaimed on the same date, and the day became a national holiday.
memorial_hu_1956_revolution_memorial_day.traditions: The day is marked with state ceremonies, wreath-laying and speeches at memorials in Budapest, including Kossuth Square and Plot 301 in the New Public Cemetery, where executed participants were buried. Flags are displayed across the country, often the 1956 flag with the communist coat of arms cut out of its centre. Museums and schools hold exhibitions and readings, and candles are lit at memorial plaques.
funFacts: Protesters cut the communist coat of arms out of the Hungarian flag; the flag with a hole became the revolution's best-known symbol.
23 October is also the date on which the Third Hungarian Republic was proclaimed, in 1989.
It is one of only three national holidays named in Hungary's constitution, alongside 15 March and 20 August.

memorial_il_yom_hashoah.intro: Yom HaShoah, on the 27th of Nisan in the Jewish calendar, is Israel's day of remembrance for the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust and for the heroism of those who resisted.
memorial_il_yom_hashoah.history: The Knesset established the day in 1951, and in 1959 it became a national memorial day by law. The date lies a week after Passover and a week before Israel's Memorial Day, and was chosen to fall close to the anniversary of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising of April 1943.
memorial_il_yom_hashoah.traditions: At 10 a.m. sirens sound for two minutes across Israel and everything comes to a halt, even traffic on the motorways. The state ceremony takes place at Yad Vashem in Jerusalem on the eve of the day, where six survivors light six torches. Places of entertainment close, and names of victims are read aloud.
funFacts: The full name of the day is 'Day of Remembrance of the Holocaust and Heroism'.
The 'March of the Living' brings thousands of young people from Auschwitz to Birkenau on this day each year.
Yad Vashem's central names database commemorates millions of Jews murdered in the Holocaust and preserves their biographical details.

memorial_il_yom_hazikaron.intro: Yom HaZikaron, on the 4th of Iyar, is Israel's Memorial Day for fallen soldiers and victims of terrorism. It ends at sunset as Independence Day begins.
memorial_il_yom_hazikaron.history: Israel first marked the fallen of the 1948 war on Independence Day itself; from 1951 the day of remembrance was moved to the eve of the celebrations. It was enshrined in law in 1963. Since 1998 victims of terrorist attacks have been commemorated on the same day.
memorial_il_yom_hazikaron.traditions: A siren sounds for one minute at 8 p.m. on the eve and for two minutes at 11 a.m. on the day, when the country stands still. Ceremonies are held at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem and at military cemeteries, and families visit the graves. Television and radio broadcast only sombre programmes.
funFacts: The transition from mourning to celebration at sunset is deliberate: Israel's independence is understood as the price paid by the fallen.
The state ceremony at the Western Wall on the eve opens with the lowering of the flag to half mast.
A red flower, the 'blood of the Maccabees' (Helichrysum), is the symbol of the day and is worn as a sticker.

memorial_in_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day, Shaheed Diwas, is observed across India on 30 January. It marks the assassination of Mahatma Gandhi in 1948 and honours all those who gave their lives for the country.
memorial_in_martyrs_day.history: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, known as Mahatma Gandhi, was shot dead on 30 January 1948 at Birla House in New Delhi by Nathuram Godse, months after India became independent. The anniversary was set aside as a national day of remembrance for Gandhi and for the country's martyrs, and is also called Sarvodaya Day. India marks several other Martyrs' Days as well, among them 23 March for Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev Thapar and Shivaram Rajguru, executed in 1931, and 21 October, Police Martyrs' Day.
memorial_in_martyrs_day.traditions: A two-minute silence is kept throughout the country at eleven in the morning. The President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Defence Minister gather at Raj Ghat in Delhi, Gandhi's memorial, to lay wreaths of flowers. A guard drawn from the armed services reverses arms as a mark of respect and buglers sound the Last Post, followed by multi-faith prayers and the singing of Gandhi's favourite hymns.
funFacts: The day is also known as Sarvodaya Day, after Gandhi's ideal of the welfare and uplift of all.
A two-minute silence is observed nationwide at eleven in the morning.
India marks several Martyrs' Days; 23 March recalls Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev Thapar and Shivaram Rajguru, executed in 1931.

memorial_it_giorno_del_ricordo.intro: The Day of Remembrance, Giorno del Ricordo, is observed in Italy on 10 February. It commemorates the victims of the foibe killings and the Istrian-Dalmatian exodus that followed the Second World War on Italy's eastern border.
memorial_it_giorno_del_ricordo.history: At the end of the war, territories on Italy's north-eastern border passed to Yugoslavia. Italians were killed in the upheaval, some of them thrown into the karst sinkholes known as foibe, and a great many left Istria, Rijeka and Dalmatia in the years that followed; estimates of both the killings and the exodus differ considerably between sources. Italy established the Day of Remembrance by Law 92 of 30 March 2004, choosing 10 February because the Paris Peace Treaties, which transferred the territories, were signed on that date in 1947.
memorial_it_giorno_del_ricordo.traditions: A state ceremony is held at the Quirinal Palace in Rome, where the president addresses relatives of the victims and commemorative medals are presented to families. Wreaths are laid at the foiba of Basovizza near Trieste, the main national memorial, and mayors hold ceremonies in towns throughout the country. Schools devote lessons to the exodus, and exhibitions and concerts of remembrance are organised. It is a civil observance, not a day off work.
funFacts: The date recalls the signing of the Paris Peace Treaties on 10 February 1947.
Law 92 of 2004 also created a commemorative medal for relatives of the victims.
The foiba of Basovizza, near Trieste, serves as the principal national memorial site.

memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.intro: Japan observes 15 August as the day for mourning the war dead and praying for peace. It marks the announcement in 1945 that Japan would accept the Allied terms, bringing the Second World War to an end.
memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.history: On 15 August 1945 a recorded address by Emperor Hirohito, later known as the Jewel Voice Broadcast, was transmitted by radio, telling the public that the government had accepted the Potsdam Declaration. The formal instrument of surrender was signed aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on 2 September. The anniversary had long been observed informally when the Japanese cabinet gave it official standing in 1982 as a day for mourning the war dead and praying for peace.
memorial_jp_end_of_war_memorial_day.traditions: A national memorial ceremony is held at the Nippon Budokan in Tokyo, attended by the emperor and empress, the prime minister and relatives of the dead. At noon a minute of silence is observed across the country, marked by a siren or chime and broadcast live. Families visit graves and memorials, lanterns are floated on rivers in some regions, and broadcasters devote the day to accounts of the war years.
funFacts: The broadcast of 15 August 1945 was the first time most people in Japan had heard the emperor's voice.
In Japanese the day is called Shusen-kinenbi, the anniversary of the end of the war.
The formal surrender documents were signed later, on 2 September 1945, in Tokyo Bay.

memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.intro: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Day is observed in Japan on 6 August. It marks the atomic bombing of Hiroshima in 1945 and remembers those who died in the attack and later from its effects.
memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.history: An atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima on the morning of 6 August 1945, destroying much of the city. Many people were killed at once and many more died afterwards from injuries and radiation; the full number is not precisely known. The first Peace Memorial Ceremony was held in 1947 by the then mayor, Shinzo Hamai, and the area near the point of detonation was rebuilt as the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park. The ceremony has since become the focus of the city's yearly appeal for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
memorial_jp_hiroshima_peace_memorial_day.traditions: The ceremony takes place at the Memorial Cenotaph in the Peace Memorial Park, with bereaved families, residents, national representatives and visitors from abroad present. At 8.15 in the morning, the moment of the detonation, the Peace Bell sounds and a minute of silent prayer is kept. A register listing those who have died is placed in the cenotaph, water and flowers are offered, doves are released and the mayor reads a Peace Declaration.
funFacts: The first Peace Memorial Ceremony was held in 1947, organised by the mayor of Hiroshima at the time, Shinzo Hamai.
The Peace Bell is rung at 8.15 in the morning, the time the bomb detonated over the city in 1945.
A register of the names of the dead is updated each year and placed inside the Memorial Cenotaph.

memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.intro: Nagasaki Peace Memorial Day is held on 9 August, the anniversary of the atomic bombing of the Japanese city in 1945. The ceremony in Nagasaki remembers those who were killed and those who survived, and renews the city's call for the abolition of nuclear weapons.
memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.history: On the morning of 9 August 1945 a United States aircraft dropped an atomic bomb over the Urakami district of Nagasaki at 11:02; the intended target, Kokura, had been obscured by cloud. Estimates of the number who died by the end of that year range from about 60,000 to 80,000, and many more suffered lasting effects. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. The ground around the hypocentre was laid out as a memorial park, where the Peace Statue by Seibo Kitamura was completed in 1955, and the city holds its peace memorial ceremony there each 9 August.
memorial_jp_nagasaki_peace_memorial_day.traditions: The ceremony takes place in Peace Park, attended by the mayor, survivors, bereaved families and representatives of many countries. A silence is observed at 11:02, the time of the blast, and a bell is rung. The mayor reads the Peace Declaration, calling for nuclear disarmament, and water is offered in memory of those who died of thirst. In the evening lanterns are floated and candles are lit at the hypocentre.
funFacts: The silence in Nagasaki is observed at 11:02, the moment of the explosion on 9 August 1945.
The ten-metre Peace Statue by Seibo Kitamura raises one hand towards the sky and stretches the other out for peace.
Nagasaki's Fountain of Peace, opened in 1969, remembers those who died searching for water.

memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.intro: South Korea observes 18 May as the memorial day of the Gwangju Democratic Uprising. It remembers the citizens of Gwangju and South Jeolla Province who died in 1980 while demanding an end to military rule and the lifting of martial law.
memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.history: In May 1980 the military government extended martial law across South Korea and closed the universities. Student protests in Gwangju that began on 18 May were met with force by paratroopers, residents joined the demonstrations, and for several days the city was held by its own citizens before troops retook it on 27 May. Estimates of the number killed vary considerably. The uprising was officially reassessed in the following decades, and 18 May was designated a national memorial day in 1997.
memorial_kr_gwangju_democratization_move.traditions: The government ceremony is held each 18 May in Gwangju, at the May 18th National Cemetery or at the Democracy Square in front of the former provincial office building, often with the president in attendance. Bereaved families, participants in the uprising, officials and students take part, and the programme includes a commemorative address, memorial performances and the collective singing of March for the Beloved. Wreaths are laid at the cemetery throughout the day.
funFacts: Archives documenting the uprising were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2011.
March for the Beloved is sung at the ceremony and is the movement's best-known song.
Victims were first buried at Mangwol-dong; the May 18th National Cemetery was later built nearby.

memorial_kr_memorial_day.intro: Memorial Day (Hyeonchungil) on 6 June honours the soldiers and civilians who died for South Korea, especially in the Korean War of 1950 to 1953.
memorial_kr_memorial_day.history: The day was established in 1956, three years after the armistice, to remember the fallen of the war. The date follows the traditional calendar, on which early June marks the start of the season for tending ancestral graves.
memorial_kr_memorial_day.traditions: At 10 a.m. a siren sounds nationwide for one minute of silence. The president leads a ceremony at the Seoul National Cemetery, where families lay flowers on the graves, and flags are flown at half mast throughout the country.
funFacts: The Korean War has never formally ended; only an armistice was signed in 1953.
The Seoul National Cemetery in Dongjak-gu is the resting place of more than 160,000 people.
Because it is a day of mourning, the national flag is raised to half mast rather than full height.

memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.intro: Freedom Defenders' Day, Laisves gyneju diena, is marked in Lithuania on 13 January. It honours the unarmed civilians killed when Soviet forces moved against the television tower and broadcasting centre in Vilnius in 1991, as the country defended its restored independence.
memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.history: Lithuania declared the restoration of its independence in March 1990. During the night of 12 to 13 January 1991 Soviet troops and armoured vehicles moved on the Vilnius television tower and the radio and television building, where crowds had gathered unarmed to protect them. Fourteen people were killed and more than a hundred were injured. Crowds went on guarding the parliament building for weeks afterwards. Lithuania later made 13 January a state day of commemoration, and the Seimas awards an annual Freedom Prize on the anniversary.
memorial_lt_freedom_defenders_day.traditions: Households across Lithuania light candles in their windows on the morning of the anniversary, and the national flag is flown with a black ribbon attached. Bonfires burn at the television tower and outside the Seimas, which holds a ceremonial sitting and presents the Freedom Prize. Flowers are laid at the victims' graves at Antakalnis Cemetery in Vilnius, and forget-me-not pins are worn as a sign of remembrance.
funFacts: The forget-me-not flower has become the emblem of remembrance for the events of January 1991.
The national flag is flown with a black mourning ribbon attached on Freedom Defenders' Day.
The victims of the January events are buried at Antakalnis Cemetery in Vilnius, where ceremonies are held each year.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.intro: 20 January remembers the defenders of the barricades of January 1991, when people in Riga protected the young Latvian democracy against Soviet special forces.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.history: After the Soviet crackdown in Vilnius on 13 January 1991, tens of thousands of Latvians built barricades around the parliament, the television centre and the bridges of Riga. On 20 January the OMON special police stormed the Interior Ministry; five people were killed, among them two cameramen filming the events.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_defende.traditions: Bonfires are lit on Dome Square in Old Riga as they were in 1991, and wreaths are laid at the memorial stones in Bastejkalns park where the victims fell. The Barricades Museum in Old Riga keeps the memory alive with original film footage.
funFacts: The barricades were built from trucks, tractors and concrete blocks brought in from all over Latvia.
Farmers kept the defenders supplied with hot food and firewood for days.
The Barricades Museum was opened in 2001 in a house on Krāmu iela in Old Riga.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.intro: 4 July commemorates the genocide against the Jews of Latvia during the German occupation, in which around 70,000 Latvian Jews were murdered.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.history: On 4 July 1941 the Great Choral Synagogue in Riga was set on fire with people inside, as were other synagogues in the city. Mass shootings followed, above all at Rumbula and Biķernieki in late 1941. The remembrance day was established in 1990.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_genocid.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the ruins of the Great Choral Synagogue on Gogoļa iela and at the Rumbula and Biķernieki memorials. The Žanis Lipke Memorial honours Latvians who hid Jews at the risk of their own lives.
funFacts: Žanis Lipke, a Riga dock worker, saved more than 50 Jews and is honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.
The memorial at the synagogue ruins includes a wall of names of the rescuers.
Before the war about 93,000 Jews lived in Latvia, roughly five percent of the population.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.intro: 14 June remembers the victims of communist terror, in particular the mass deportation of 14 June 1941, when more than 15,000 people were taken from Latvia to Siberia in a single night.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.history: On the night of 13 to 14 June 1941 the Soviet authorities arrested families across Latvia, separated men from women and children and sent them east in freight wagons. Many did not survive the first winter. A second, even larger deportation followed on 25 March 1949, which is also a day of remembrance.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.traditions: Flags fly with black ribbons, and wreaths are laid at Torņakalns railway station in Riga, from where the trains left. Names of the deported are read aloud, and the Museum of the Occupation holds a memorial event.
funFacts: A memorial wagon at Torņakalns station shows the conditions of the deportations.
Together the deportations of 1941 and 1949 affected almost 60,000 people in Latvia.
In 1987 a flower-laying at the Freedom Monument on 14 June became one of the first public protests of the Latvian independence movement.

memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.intro: On the first Sunday of December Latvia remembers the Latvians killed during the Soviet 'Latvian Operation' of 1937 and 1938 and all victims of the communist regime.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.history: On 3 December 1937 the Soviet secret police NKVD began the 'Latvian Operation', in which more than 22,000 Latvians living in the Soviet Union were arrested and some 16,000 shot. The remembrance day recalls this and the later repressions after 1940.
memorial_lv_commemoration_day_of_victims.traditions: Memorial services are held at the Freedom Monument in Riga and in churches, and candles are lit at memorials. The Museum of the Occupation and historians present research on the fate of the victims.
funFacts: The Latvian Operation was one of several 'national operations' of the Great Terror.
Many of the victims were descendants of Latvian farmers who had settled in Russia in the 19th century.
The memorial site at Levashovo near St Petersburg holds a monument to the Latvian victims.

memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.intro: 23 August is the European Day of Remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism, the anniversary of the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact of 1939 and of the Baltic Way of 1989.
memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.history: On 23 August 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe, which sealed the fate of the Baltic states. Fifty years later, on 23 August 1989, about two million people formed a human chain from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius to demand independence.
memorial_lv_day_of_remembrance_for_victi.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Freedom Monument in Riga, and candles are lit in memory of the victims of both regimes. The Baltic Way is recalled with exhibitions and films, and the day is marked across the European Union.
funFacts: The Baltic Way stretched about 675 kilometres across the three countries.
The documents of the Baltic Way were added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2009.
In 2008 the European Parliament called for 23 August to become a day of remembrance for the victims of Stalinism and Nazism.

memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.intro: Heroes' Commemoration Day on 22 June recalls the Battle of Cēsis in 1919, a turning point of the Latvian War of Independence.
memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.history: Between 19 and 23 June 1919 Estonian troops and Latvian units defeated the German Baltic Landeswehr near Cēsis. The victory ended German plans to control the Baltic and secured the government of Kārlis Ulmanis. Estonia celebrates the same battle on 23 June as Victory Day.
memorial_lv_heroes_commemoration_day_ann.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the monument to the fallen in Cēsis and at the Brothers' Cemetery in Riga. Latvian and Estonian officials often commemorate the battle together.
funFacts: Latvian schoolboys from Cēsis fought in the battle as a volunteer company.
Cēsis Castle, one of the best-preserved medieval castles in Latvia, overlooks the town.
The battle is sometimes called the 'Battle of Võnnu' in Estonia, after the Estonian name of Cēsis.

memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.intro: 11 August honours the freedom fighters of the Latvian War of Independence and marks the peace treaty with Soviet Russia of 1920 that ended the war.
memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.history: In the Treaty of Riga of 11 August 1920 Soviet Russia recognised Latvia's independence 'for all time'. The war of 1918 to 1920 had been fought against Bolshevik forces, German units and the West Russian Volunteer Army. About 3,000 Latvian soldiers died.
memorial_lv_latvian_freedom_fighters_rem.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the Freedom Monument and at the Brothers' Cemetery in Riga, where the fallen of the war are buried. The National Armed Forces hold a ceremony, and veterans' organisations remember the volunteers.
funFacts: The Brothers' Cemetery in Riga was designed by sculptor Kārlis Zāle, who also created the Freedom Monument.
The Freedom Monument, unveiled in 1935, bears the inscription 'For Fatherland and Freedom'.
The Soviet Union broke the 'eternal' peace treaty twenty years later with the occupation of 1940.

memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.intro: 2 March remembers the Latvian national partisans, the 'Forest Brothers', who fought against the Soviet occupation after 1944.
memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.history: The date recalls the Battle of Stompaki on 2 and 3 March 1945 in Latgale, the largest engagement between Latvian partisans and Soviet forces. Around 20,000 Latvians took part in the armed resistance, which lasted into the 1950s. The remembrance day was added to the law in 2020.
memorial_lv_national_partisan_armed_resi.traditions: Wreaths are laid at partisan memorials and bunkers in the forests, and the National Armed Forces hold ceremonies. Local museums and historians tell the stories of individual resistance groups.
funFacts: At Stompaki about 350 partisans held out against several thousand Soviet troops before breaking out of the encirclement.
The last known Latvian partisan came out of hiding only in the 1990s.
Similar days of remembrance exist in Estonia and Lithuania.

memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.intro: 17 March honours the national resistance movement, above all the Latvian Central Council, which demanded the restoration of independence during the German occupation in 1944.
memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.history: On 17 March 1944, 188 leading Latvian politicians and public figures signed a memorandum calling for the restoration of the independent Republic of Latvia. The Central Council was led by Konstantīns Čakste, who was arrested by the Gestapo and died in a concentration camp in 1945.
memorial_lv_national_resistance_movement.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the memorial plaque to the Central Council in Riga, and the president or speaker of parliament gives a commemorative address. Historians recall the many forms of resistance to both occupying powers.
funFacts: Konstantīns Čakste was the son of Latvia's first president, Jānis Čakste.
The Central Council also organised boat crossings that helped refugees escape to Sweden.
The memorandum was smuggled out of the country and handed to the Western Allies.

memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.intro: 21 November remembers the 54 people who died when the roof of a supermarket collapsed in the Zolitūde district of Riga in 2013.
memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.history: On the evening of 21 November 2013 the roof of a Maxima supermarket collapsed during shopping hours; among the dead were three firefighters killed when a second section fell during the rescue. It was the deadliest disaster in Latvia since independence and led to stricter building rules.
memorial_lv_remembrance_day_of_the_trage.traditions: A memorial service is held at the memorial in Zolitūde, and candles are lit at the site. Flags fly at half mast, and the names of the victims are read aloud.
funFacts: The prime minister resigned six days after the disaster, taking political responsibility.
The memorial at the site bears the names of all 54 victims.
Latvia declared three days of national mourning after the disaster, from 23 to 25 November 2013.

memorial_mg_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day in Madagascar is observed on 29 March. It remembers those who died in the Malagasy uprising against French colonial rule, which began on that date in 1947, and in the repression that followed it.
memorial_mg_martyrs_day.history: On the evening of 29 March 1947 Malagasy nationalists launched coordinated attacks on military posts and French-owned plantations in the east of the island, around Moramanga and Manakara. The rising spread across a large part of Madagascar and was put down by French forces over nearly two years, ending in 1949; estimates of the number of dead vary widely between sources. In 1967 the Malagasy government declared 29 March a day of mourning, and official commemorations have been held annually since then.
memorial_mg_martyrs_day.traditions: The day is a public holiday observed as a day of mourning. The president and other officials lay wreaths at monuments to the dead, and a central ceremony is held at Moramanga, where the uprising began. Churches hold services, schools and broadcasters revisit the events of 1947, and the museum dedicated to the uprising in Moramanga receives visitors throughout the day.
funFacts: The uprising began on the evening of 29 March 1947 in the east of the island.
A national museum devoted to the uprising was inaugurated in Moramanga in 2012.
Madagascar became independent from France on 26 June 1960.

memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.intro: Genocide Remembrance Day on 28 May commemorates the Ovaherero and Nama who were killed under German colonial rule between 1904 and 1908.
memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.history: After the uprising of 1904 the German colonial army drove the Herero into the Omaheke desert and imprisoned survivors in camps such as Shark Island. Tens of thousands died. Germany officially recognised the events as genocide in 2021. Namibia observed the day for the first time in 2025, choosing the date on which the camps were ordered closed in 1907.
memorial_na_genocide_remembrance_day.traditions: A national ceremony with a minute of silence and candle lighting is held, and descendants of the victims hold memorial gatherings in Okahandja, Swakopmund and Lüderitz. The day is a public holiday.
funFacts: The genocide of the Herero and Nama is considered the first genocide of the 20th century.
In 2018 Germany returned human remains that had been taken to Berlin for racial research.
The Genocide Memorial in Windhoek was unveiled in 2014 on the site of the former equestrian monument to German colonial soldiers.

memorial_na_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day is a public holiday in Namibia, observed on 26 August. It honours those who died in the struggle for Namibian independence and marks the first armed clash of the liberation war, which took place at Omugulugwombashe in 1966.
memorial_na_heroes_day.history: In 1966 the United Nations General Assembly ended South Africa's mandate over South West Africa, but South African rule continued. SWAPO had formed its armed wing, the People's Liberation Army of Namibia, in 1962 and established a camp at Omugulugwombashe in the north. On 26 August 1966 South African forces attacked the camp in the first battle of the Namibian War of Independence. The war lasted until the end of the 1980s, and Namibia became independent in 1990. The anniversary is now a national holiday and is known internationally as Namibia Day.
memorial_na_heroes_day.traditions: The main ceremony is held at Heroes' Acre, the national memorial south of Windhoek, where the president lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and addresses the nation. Military parades, the laying of flowers and the awarding of medals to veterans form part of the programme. Commemorations are also held in the north and at regional memorials, with church services and readings of the names of the fallen.
funFacts: Heroes' Acre, the national memorial outside Windhoek, was inaugurated on Heroes' Day in 2002.
The United Nations marks 26 August as Namibia Day.
The first battle of the independence war took place at Omugulugwombashe on 26 August 1966.

memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.intro: Dodenherdenking, the Remembrance of the Dead, is held in the Netherlands every 4 May. It remembers all Dutch civilians and members of the armed forces who have died in wars and peacekeeping missions since the outbreak of the Second World War, and precedes Liberation Day on 5 May.
memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.history: The Netherlands was occupied by Germany from 1940 until the surrender of German forces in the country in May 1945. Commemorations of the war dead began in the first years after the liberation and were given a fixed national form on 4 May, the eve of Liberation Day. At first only Dutch victims of the Second World War were remembered; since 1961 the commemoration has also included those who died in later conflicts and in peacekeeping operations, among them the Indonesian war, Lebanon and Bosnia.
memorial_nl_remembrance_of_the_dead.traditions: Flags fly at half-mast from six in the evening. At eight o'clock the whole country observes two minutes of silence: trains and traffic stop, broadcasts fall quiet and people stand still in the street. The central ceremony is at the National Monument on Dam Square in Amsterdam, where the king and queen lay a wreath, and it is broadcast live. Afterwards the flags are raised again while the national anthem is played, and flowers are laid at local monuments.
funFacts: The two minutes of silence begin at eight in the evening, and public transport across the country comes to a halt.
Flags fly at half-mast from six in the evening until the silence ends, then are raised while the anthem plays.
Liberation Day follows on 5 May, marking the German surrender in the Netherlands in 1945.

memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.intro: In Norway, 22 July is a day of remembrance for the victims of the attacks of 2011, when a bomb was detonated in the government quarter in Oslo and a shooting took place at a Labour youth camp on the island of Utøya.
memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.history: On 22 July 2011 a car bomb exploded outside government buildings in central Oslo, killing eight people. The attacker then travelled to Utøya, where the Workers' Youth League was holding its summer camp, and killed sixty-nine more, most of them teenagers. Seventy-seven people died in all, making it the deadliest attack in Norway since the Second World War. The perpetrator was convicted and sentenced to preventive detention. The anniversary has been marked nationally every year since, with a large commemoration on the round anniversaries.
memorial_no_22_july_remembrance_day.traditions: Flags fly at half-mast. Members of the royal family, the prime minister, survivors and bereaved families attend a ceremony in the government quarter where the names of the dead are read aloud, followed by a memorial service in Oslo Cathedral and the ringing of church bells there and across the country. Flowers are laid at the Iron Roses memorial beside the cathedral and at the memorial site by Utøya.
funFacts: Seventy-seven people were killed, sixty-nine of them at the youth camp on Utøya.
The Iron Roses memorial by Oslo Cathedral holds a thousand hand-forged roses and dates from 2019.
The 22 July Centre in Oslo documents the attacks and is widely used for school visits.

memorial_pa_martyrs_day.intro: Martyrs' Day, Día de los Mártires, is a day of national mourning in Panama observed on 9 January. It remembers the Panamanians killed in January 1964 during clashes in the United States-controlled Panama Canal Zone over the right to fly the Panamanian flag there.
memorial_pa_martyrs_day.history: From 1903 the United States controlled the Canal Zone, a strip dividing Panama in two. An earlier agreement provided for both flags to fly together at civilian sites in the zone, but at Balboa High School only the American flag was raised. On 9 January 1964 students from the Instituto Nacional went to the school with a Panamanian flag; it was torn in the confrontation that followed, and unrest spread across the zone for several days. More than twenty Panamanians and several United States soldiers died. The events helped lead to the Torrijos-Carter Treaties of 1977, under which the canal passed to Panama at the end of 1999.
memorial_pa_martyrs_day.traditions: Public offices close and flags fly at half-mast. Officials, veterans' associations and student delegations lay wreaths at memorials in Panama City, above all at the former Balboa High School, now the Ascanio Arosemena Training Center, where the names of the dead are inscribed. The names are read aloud at commemorative acts, and schools hold assemblies on the history of the canal and Panamanian sovereignty.
funFacts: Ascanio Arosemena, a student killed on 9 January 1964, is remembered as the first of the martyrs.
The former Balboa High School now houses a Panama Canal training centre named after him.
Panama took full control of the canal on 31 December 1999, under treaties signed in 1977.

memorial_pg_remembrance_day.intro: Remembrance Day on 23 July honours Papua New Guineans who served and died in the Second World War, especially the soldiers of the Papuan Infantry Battalion.
memorial_pg_remembrance_day.history: On 23 July 1942 the Papuan Infantry Battalion fought its first engagement against Japanese troops near Awala at the start of the Kokoda campaign. The day became a national holiday after independence in 1975.
memorial_pg_remembrance_day.traditions: Wreaths are laid at the Bomana War Cemetery near Port Moresby and at the Remembrance Park in the capital. Veterans' families, the defence force and schoolchildren take part, and the Last Post is sounded.
funFacts: Papua New Guineans who carried wounded soldiers along the Kokoda Track became known as the 'Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels'.
Bomana War Cemetery is the largest war cemetery in the Pacific with more than 3,800 graves.
The Papuan Infantry Battalion was the first indigenous military unit of the country.

memorial_ph_day_of_valor.intro: Araw ng Kagitingan, the Day of Valor, is a national holiday in the Philippines observed on 9 April. It honours the Filipino and American soldiers who defended Bataan and Corregidor in 1942 and those who died in captivity afterwards.
memorial_ph_day_of_valor.history: On 9 April 1942 the defenders of the Bataan Peninsula surrendered to Japanese forces after months of fighting, and tens of thousands of Filipino and American troops were forced on the march to Camp O'Donnell, during which many died. Corregidor fell the following month. President Carlos P. Garcia signed Republic Act No. 3022 in 1961, making 9 April a national observance then known as Bataan Day. It was later renamed Araw ng Kagitingan, the Day of Valor. Between 1980 and 1987 the date was temporarily moved to 6 May before returning to 9 April.
memorial_ph_day_of_valor.traditions: The main national rite is held at the Mount Samat National Shrine, the Dambana ng Kagitingan, in Pilar, Bataan, where the President or a representative lays a wreath at the memorial cross. Surviving veterans, their families and diplomats from the United States and Japan usually attend, and the programme includes prayers, honours for the war dead and addresses. The day falls within Philippine Veterans Week, from 5 to 11 April.
funFacts: Dambana ng Kagitingan, the Shrine of Valor, stands on Mount Samat above the peninsula where the 1942 fighting took place.
The observance was created in 1961 as Bataan Day under Republic Act No. 3022 and later renamed Araw ng Kagitingan.
From 1980 to 1987 the day was held on 6 May before it was returned to its original date of 9 April.

memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.intro: National Heroes Day is a public holiday in the Philippines, observed on the last Monday of August. It honours the Filipinos who fought and died for the country's freedom, from the revolutionaries of 1896 to soldiers, resistance fighters and later generations.
memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.history: The date recalls the start of the Philippine Revolution against Spanish rule in late August 1896, when members of the Katipunan led by Andrés Bonifacio tore up their tax certificates in an act remembered as the Cry of Pugad Lawin, also known as the Cry of Balintawak. Because the exact day and place remained disputed, lawmakers fixed the observance to the final week of August. Act No. 3827 of 1931 first set it on the last Sunday of August, and Republic Act No. 9492 moved it to the last Monday in 2007.
memorial_ph_national_heroes_day.traditions: The president usually leads a wreath-laying ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig, attended by an honour guard and government officials. Local governments hold their own rites at monuments and plazas, and flags are displayed at public buildings. Commemorative speeches often widen the meaning of heroism to include ordinary Filipinos such as overseas workers and health workers.
funFacts: The law names no specific heroes, leaving the day open to honour both famous figures and unnamed ones.
Act No. 3827 first established the observance in 1931, on the last Sunday of August.
Since 2007 the holiday falls on the last Monday of August, so its date shifts each year.

memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.intro: The Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Katyn Massacre is observed in Poland on 13 April. It honours the Polish officers, police officers and civilians murdered by the Soviet secret police in the spring of 1940.
memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.history: In the spring of 1940, following a decision of the Soviet Politburo, the NKVD shot thousands of Polish prisoners of war and detainees at Katyn and other sites, among them army officers, police, border guards, teachers, doctors and lawyers. On 13 April 1943 German radio announced the discovery of mass graves in the Katyn forest. The Soviet Union denied responsibility for decades and admitted it only on 13 April 1990. The Polish Sejm established the national day of remembrance by resolution in November 2007.
memorial_pl_katyn_remembrance_day.traditions: State ceremonies are held at the Katyn Museum in Warsaw and at the Polish war cemeteries at Katyn, Kharkiv and Mednoye, with wreaths, candles and a roll call of the dead. Flags are flown at half-mast with mourning ribbons and Masses are said in churches across the country. Families of the victims, officials and soldiers take part, and oak trees planted in memory of individual victims are tended in many towns.
funFacts: The graves in the Katyn forest were announced on 13 April 1943; the Soviet Union admitted responsibility on the same date in 1990.
The Polish Sejm established the national day of remembrance by resolution in November 2007.
Polish war cemeteries for the victims were opened at Katyn, Kharkiv and Mednoye.

memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.intro: Every 19 April Poland remembers the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, which began on that date in 1943. The day honours the Jewish fighters who took up arms against the German forces sent to liquidate the ghetto, and the hundreds of thousands of people murdered there and in the death camps.
memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.history: Warsaw's Jewish population was confined to a sealed ghetto in 1940. During the summer of 1942 the great majority of its inhabitants were deported to the Treblinka extermination camp. When German units returned on 19 April 1943 to complete the liquidation, the Jewish Combat Organisation under Mordechai Anielewicz and the Jewish Military Union resisted with a small stock of weapons. Fighting and the systematic burning of the district lasted until 16 May 1943. The anniversary has been marked in Warsaw since the first years after the war.
memorial_pl_warsaw_ghetto_uprising_remem.traditions: At noon sirens sound across Warsaw for one minute. Officials, survivors and their families lay flowers at the Monument to the Ghetto Heroes in Muranów and at the Umschlagplatz memorial, and walk the Path of Remembrance through the former ghetto. The POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews hands out paper daffodils, which people pin to their clothes; the flower recalls the yellow bouquets that the last surviving commander, Marek Edelman, laid at the monument each year.
funFacts: The daffodil became the symbol of the day because Marek Edelman, the last surviving commander, laid yellow flowers at the monument each year.
Sirens sound across Warsaw for one minute at noon on 19 April.
The Monument to the Ghetto Heroes, by Nathan Rapoport, was unveiled in 1948 among the ruins of the district.

memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.intro: The National Day of Remembrance of the Warsaw Uprising is marked in Poland on 1 August. It honours the insurgents and the civilians of Warsaw who died during the rising against the German occupation in 1944.
memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.history: The Warsaw Uprising began at 17:00 on 1 August 1944, the moment known as hour W, when units of the Polish Home Army under General Tadeusz Bór-Komorowski attacked German positions across the city. Colonel Antoni Chruściel commanded the forces inside Warsaw.
