The fighting lasted 63 days before the Home Army capitulated on 2 October; thousands of insurgents and far more civilians were killed, and much of the city was destroyed afterwards. Poland established 1 August as an official day of remembrance by law in 2009.
memorial_pl_warsaw_uprising_remembrance_.traditions: At 17:00 on 1 August sirens sound across Warsaw and much of Poland. Traffic stops, pedestrians stand still and many drivers step out of their cars for a minute. Wreaths are laid at the Powązki Military Cemetery and at the monuments to the uprising, veterans attend the official ceremonies, and the Warsaw Uprising Museum opens without charge. In the evening people gather in the streets to sing wartime songs.
funFacts: The starting moment is called hour W, after the Polish word wybuch, meaning outbreak.
The fighting lasted 63 days, far longer than its planners had expected.
The Warsaw Uprising Museum opened in 2004, on the sixtieth anniversary of the rising.

memorial_py_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day, Dia de los Heroes, is a national holiday in Paraguay on 1 March. It honours Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez and all Paraguayans who died in the country's wars, above all the Paraguayan War of 1864 to 1870.
memorial_py_heroes_day.history: The date recalls the Battle of Cerro Cora on 1 March 1870, the last engagement of the Paraguayan War, in which President Francisco Solano Lopez was killed after refusing to surrender. The war against the allied forces of Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay had lasted more than five years and left Paraguay devastated. Lopez was later reinterpreted in Paraguay as a national hero rather than a defeated leader, and 1 March was set aside to honour the country's war dead, with commemorative activities continuing through the month.
memorial_py_heroes_day.traditions: The central ceremony takes place at the Panteon Nacional de los Heroes in Asuncion, where the remains of Solano Lopez and other national figures rest. The President and members of the government lay wreaths, an honour guard stands watch and military honours are rendered. Wreaths are also laid at Cerro Cora National Park in Amambay, the site of the 1870 battle, and at monuments in towns across the country.
funFacts: The Battle of Cerro Cora on 1 March 1870 ended the Paraguayan War, one of the deadliest conflicts in South American history.
The Panteon Nacional de los Heroes in Asuncion holds the remains of Marshal Francisco Solano Lopez.
Cerro Cora, in the Amambay department, is preserved as a national park and place of remembrance.

memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.intro: Kwibuka, meaning remember in Kinyarwanda, is Rwanda's day of remembrance for the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi. It is observed on 7 April and opens a national mourning period that lasts about a hundred days.
memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.history: The genocide began in April 1994, after the aircraft carrying President Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down on 6 April, and continued for roughly a hundred days until the Rwandan Patriotic Front took control of the country in July. Those killed were overwhelmingly Tutsi, along with Hutu who opposed the killings; estimates of the death toll differ between sources. Rwanda has commemorated 7 April since the years immediately after the genocide, and the United Nations designated the date an international day of reflection, first observed in 2004.
memorial_rw_genocide_remembrance_day.traditions: The president lights a flame of remembrance at the Kigali Genocide Memorial in Gisozi and addresses the nation, followed by a national ceremony and a night vigil. The week after 7 April is an official week of mourning, with flags at half-mast, subdued broadcasting and music, and gatherings at memorial sites across the country. Walks of remembrance are held, and the mourning period continues until Liberation Day on 4 July.
funFacts: Kwibuka means remember in Kinyarwanda and gives the annual commemoration its name.
The mourning period runs from 7 April to Liberation Day on 4 July, about a hundred days.
The Kigali Genocide Memorial at Gisozi was inaugurated in April 2004, ten years after the genocide.

memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.intro: The Day of Uprising Against Occupation is a Slovenian state holiday marked each year on 27 April. It remembers the founding of the resistance movement that opposed the occupation and partition of Slovene territory during the Second World War.
memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.history: In April 1941 Slovene territory was occupied and partitioned by Germany, Italy and Hungary. On 26 April 1941, at the Ljubljana home of the critic Josip Vidmar, representatives of the Communist Party of Slovenia, Christian socialists, the Sokol movement and cultural figures founded the Anti-Imperialist Front, which was renamed the Liberation Front of the Slovene Nation later that year. For about two decades it was believed that the meeting had taken place on 27 April, and that date became the Day of the Liberation Front. It was kept, and the holiday renamed, after Slovenia became independent in 1991.
memorial_si_day_of_uprising_against_occu.traditions: The day is a work-free state holiday. The central state ceremony is held on the eve of the holiday, each year in a different town connected with the resistance. Across the country there are wreath-layings at partisan monuments, commemorative marches and local gatherings, while veterans' organisations, museums and schools host exhibitions and talks about the occupation years.
funFacts: The holiday falls on 27 April, although historians date the founding meeting to 26 April 1941.
Until 1991 the day was known as Day of the Liberation Front, dan Osvobodilne fronte.
The movement began under the name Anti-Imperialist Front and took its later name in 1941.

memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.intro: The Slovak National Uprising Anniversary is a public holiday in Slovakia on 29 August. It marks the day in 1944 when Slovak soldiers and partisans rose in arms against Nazi German occupation and the collaborationist wartime Slovak regime.
memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.history: The uprising began on 29 August 1944 and was directed by the Slovak National Council, which brought together communist and non-communist resistance groups. Lieutenant Colonel Jan Golian led the insurgent forces at first, and Division General Rudolf Viest took command on 7 October. The insurgents briefly controlled a large part of Slovak territory before German units pushed them back and took Banska Bystrica on 27 October 1944. Fighters then continued in the mountains as partisans until the country was liberated in spring 1945. The anniversary is today a national holiday.
memorial_sk_slovak_national_uprising_ann.traditions: Official ceremonies centre on Banska Bystrica, the insurgent capital of 1944, where the Museum of the Slovak National Uprising and its monument stand. State representatives lay wreaths, military honours are rendered and veterans' associations take part. Wreath-layings, exhibitions and commemorative marches are also held at partisan memorials and village monuments across Slovakia, and public buildings display the national flag.
funFacts: The uprising lasted about two months, from 29 August 1944 to the fall of Banska Bystrica on 27 October 1944.
The Museum of the Slovak National Uprising was founded in 1955; its distinctive split building in Banska Bystrica was completed in 1969.
After the uprising was suppressed, its fighters kept up resistance in the mountains until liberation in April 1945.

memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.intro: 17 November commemorates the students' protests of 1939 and 1989 and the beginning of the Velvet Revolution that ended communist rule in Czechoslovakia.
memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.history: On 17 November 1939 the Nazi occupiers closed Czech universities and executed nine student leaders. On 17 November 1989 a student demonstration in Prague was violently dispersed, triggering the mass protests of the Velvet Revolution. In Slovakia the anniversary remains a state holiday, but is not a day off work.
memorial_sk_struggle_for_freedom_and_dem.traditions: Gatherings with candles and speeches are held in Bratislava and other towns, and people ring keys as they did in 1989. Concerts and discussions with participants of the revolution take place, and the day is also International Students' Day.
funFacts: Jingling keys became the sound of the Velvet Revolution, symbolising the message 'time to go' to the communists.
In Bratislava the first large demonstration took place on the Square of the Slovak National Uprising.
Alexander Dubček, the face of the 1968 Prague Spring, returned to public life during the revolution.

memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.intro: On 2 November, All Souls' Day, San Marino commemorates all those who died in war, together with the Catholic remembrance of the dead.
memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.history: The tiny republic remained neutral in both world wars but was bombed by mistake by British aircraft in June 1944, killing 63 people, and took in about 100,000 refugees. The commemoration on All Souls' Day is one of the country's official holidays.
memorial_sm_commemoration_of_all_those_w.traditions: Families visit the cemeteries, above all Montalbo cemetery, and lay flowers and light candles on the graves. A ceremony honours the war dead of the republic, and the Captains Regent take part in a memorial mass.
funFacts: San Marino's population is only about 34,000, so almost every family had relatives among the wartime refugees.
A plaque at the railway station remembers the victims of the 1944 bombing.
All Souls' Day has been observed by the Catholic Church since the 11th century.

memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.intro: Atatürk Memorial Day is observed throughout Turkey on 10 November, the anniversary of the death of Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1938. The founder and first president of the Turkish Republic is remembered at the exact hour of his death with a silence kept across the whole country.
memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.history: Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish national movement after the First World War and became the first president of the republic proclaimed in 1923, carrying through far-reaching reforms of the state, the law, the alphabet and education. His health declined through 1938, and he died of cirrhosis of the liver at 09:05 on 10 November 1938 at Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul. A state funeral was held in Ankara on 21 November, with delegations from seventeen countries. His remains were moved to the Anıtkabir mausoleum in Ankara on the anniversary of his death in 1953.
memorial_tr_ataturk_memorial_day.traditions: At 09:05 sirens sound across the country and everything stops: people rise from their desks, traffic halts and drivers step out of their cars for the silence, which is followed by the national anthem. Flags fly at half-mast, and the president, ministers and military commanders lay a wreath at Anıtkabir, where large crowds file past through the day. Schools hold memorial assemblies with speeches, poems and readings.
funFacts: The silence begins at 09:05, the exact time of Atatürk's death on 10 November 1938.
He was laid to rest at Anıtkabir in Ankara in 1953, after fifteen years in the city's Ethnography Museum.
At Dolmabahçe Palace in Istanbul, where he died, the clock in his room is kept at 09:05.

memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.intro: Ukraine marks 26 April as the day of remembrance for the Chernobyl disaster. It honours those who died in the 1986 accident at the nuclear power plant, the emergency workers who contained its aftermath and the residents who lost their homes.
memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.history: At 01:23 on 26 April 1986 reactor number four of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant, near the city of Pripyat in what was then the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, was destroyed during a test. Firefighters and plant staff were exposed to severe radiation, and Pripyat was evacuated the following day, its residents leaving with few belongings. Hundreds of thousands of workers, later known as liquidators, took part in the clean-up. In 2016 the United Nations designated 26 April as an international remembrance day.
memorial_ua_chernobyl_remembrance_day.traditions: Commemorations begin at night. In Slavutych, the town built for the displaced plant workers, people gather in the central square shortly after midnight, place candles and flowers before the memorial, and a bell is rung at the hour of the accident. Church services are held in Chernobyl and Kyiv, wreaths are laid at monuments to the firefighters and liquidators, and flags fly at half-mast.
funFacts: The reactor was destroyed at 01:23 at night, the hour at which memorial bells are rung.
Pripyat was evacuated on 27 April 1986, the day after the accident, and has stood empty since.
The United Nations designated 26 April International Chernobyl Disaster Remembrance Day in 2016.

memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.intro: Holodomor Remembrance Day is observed in Ukraine on the fourth Saturday of November. It remembers the victims of the famine of 1932 and 1933, when millions of Ukrainians starved to death under Soviet rule, and of the other famines of the Soviet period.
memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.history: Grain requisitions and the forced collectivisation of agriculture stripped Ukrainian villages of food through the winter of 1932 and the spring of 1933, while people were prevented from leaving to look for it. Millions died; the exact number remains disputed. For decades the famine could not be spoken of publicly. President Leonid Kuchma created a national day of remembrance by decree in 1998. Its name was widened in 2000 and 2004 to include the famines of 1921 to 1923 and 1946 to 1947, and narrowed again in 2007 to focus on the Holodomor.
memorial_ua_holodomor_remembrance_day.traditions: At four in the afternoon the country observes a minute of silence, and people light a candle and set it in the window at home. Flags fly at half-mast and entertainment programmes are suspended. Ceremonies are held at the National Museum of the Holodomor-Genocide in Kyiv, where officials lay ears of wheat and symbolic vessels of grain, memorial services take place in churches, and candles are placed at monuments in villages across the country.
funFacts: Candles are lit at four in the afternoon and placed in windows across Ukraine.
The day falls on the fourth Saturday of November, so its date changes each year.
Canada has observed a Ukrainian Famine and Genocide Memorial Day on the same date since 2008.

memorial_ug_martyrs_day.intro: Uganda Martyrs Day is a public holiday in Uganda on 3 June. It remembers the Catholic and Anglican converts put to death in the kingdom of Buganda in the 1880s, among them Charles Lwanga and his companions, who died on that date in 1886.
memorial_ug_martyrs_day.history: Between 1885 and 1887 a group of Christian converts at the court of Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda were executed for refusing to renounce their faith. Twenty-two were Catholic and twenty-three Anglican. The largest group, including Charles Lwanga, died on 3 June 1886 at Namugongo. The Catholic martyrs were beatified in 1920 and canonised by Pope Paul VI at St Peter's Basilica in Rome on 18 October 1964, and 3 June entered the General Roman Calendar as their feast day.
memorial_ug_martyrs_day.traditions: Pilgrims travel to the shrines at Namugongo outside Kampala, where a Catholic basilica built in 1968 and an Anglican memorial site stand close together. Many walk for days from across Uganda and from neighbouring countries to reach them. Open-air Masses and Anglican services are held on the day, and the Munyonyo Martyrs' Shrine near Kampala also draws visitors. Both churches mark the anniversary on the same date.
funFacts: The Catholic martyrs were beatified in 1920 and canonised on 18 October 1964 by Pope Paul VI in Rome.
The Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo was built in 1968 and has drawn large pilgrimages since the 1980s.
The Munyonyo Martyrs' Shrine was raised as a thanksgiving monument for the canonisation of the martyrs.

memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.intro: The International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery and the Transatlantic Slave Trade is observed worldwide on 25 March. Established by the United Nations, it honours the millions of African men, women and children who were enslaved and shipped across the Atlantic over some four centuries.
memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.history: The transatlantic slave trade carried captive Africans to the Americas from the sixteenth to the nineteenth century, and the United Nations describes it as one of the gravest violations of human rights in history. The General Assembly designated 25 March as an annual day of remembrance in 2007, the year in which two hundred years had passed since Britain abolished its slave trade. The day was first observed in 2008 under the theme 'Breaking the Silence, Lest We Forget', and each year since has been given its own theme.
memorial_un_remembrance_of_victims_of_sl.traditions: The General Assembly holds a commemorative meeting at United Nations Headquarters in New York, with descendants of the enslaved, scholars, artists and diplomats taking part. Flowers and wreaths are laid at the Ark of Return, the permanent memorial in the visitors' plaza. Member states, schools, museums and UNESCO mark the day with lectures, exhibitions, concerts and readings on the history of slavery and its consequences today.
funFacts: The Ark of Return, the permanent memorial at United Nations Headquarters, was unveiled in 2015.
It was designed by the Haitian-American architect Rodney Leon, who also designed New York's African Burial Ground memorial.
The first observance in 2008 carried the theme 'Breaking the Silence, Lest We Forget'.

memorial_us_memorial_day.intro: Memorial Day on the last Monday in May is the U.S. day of remembrance for fallen American soldiers. It is also the unofficial start of summer in the U.S.
memorial_us_memorial_day.history: The day grew out of the American Civil War (1861–1865), in which over 600,000 soldiers died. In May 1868 General John A. Logan ordered a ‘Decoration Day' on which the graves of fallen soldiers were to be decorated with flowers. The custom spread after both World Wars and today commemorates all U.S. soldiers who fell in war. In 1971 the day was officially moved to the last Monday in May — to create a long weekend.
memorial_us_memorial_day.traditions: At Arlington National Cemetery the President lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. Families visit graves, decorating them with flags and flowers. At 3 p.m. local time the ‘National Moment of Remembrance' calls for a moment of silence nationwide. There are also traditional parades, barbecues and the Indianapolis 500 motor race.
funFacts: Arlington National Cemetery is the resting place of service members, veterans and eligible family members, not only those killed in war.
The red poppy became a symbol of remembrance after World War I — inspired by the poem ‘In Flanders Fields'.
The first Indianapolis 500 took place on 30 May 1911. Today the race is traditionally part of Memorial Day weekend.
The older name ‘Decoration Day’ refers to decorating graves. The name ‘Memorial Day’ was already in use long before 1971.

memorial_us_patriot_day.intro: Patriot Day is observed in the United States on 11 September in memory of those killed in the terrorist attacks of 2001. It is a national day of remembrance rather than a federal holiday, so schools and offices remain open.
memorial_us_patriot_day.history: On 11 September 2001 hijacked airliners were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York and into the Pentagon, while a fourth aircraft came down in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Thousands of people were killed, among them many firefighters, police officers and other emergency responders. Legislation introduced shortly afterwards by Representative Vito Fossella led to the first Patriot Day being proclaimed for 11 September 2002, and every president since has issued an annual proclamation.
memorial_us_patriot_day.traditions: Flags on public buildings and at private homes are lowered to half-staff, and a moment of silence is observed at 8:46 a.m. Eastern time, the minute the first aircraft struck. Ceremonies take place at the National September 11 Memorial in New York, at the Pentagon and at the Flight 93 National Memorial near Shanksville, where the names of the dead are read aloud. The date is also observed as a National Day of Service and Remembrance.
funFacts: Patriot Day is a day of remembrance, not a federal holiday, so it is a normal working day.
The New York ceremony pauses six times, marking each impact and each tower's collapse.
Patriot Day is distinct from Patriots' Day, which is marked in April in Massachusetts and Maine.

memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.intro: National Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day is observed in the United States on 7 December. It honours the service members and civilians killed in the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, in 1941, the event that brought the country into the Second World War.
memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.history: On the morning of 7 December 1941 Japanese aircraft attacked the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on Oahu. More than two thousand Americans were killed and many ships and aircraft were destroyed or damaged. The United States entered the war the following day. Congress designated 7 December as National Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day in 1994 under Public Law 103-308; President Bill Clinton signed the joint resolution on 23 August 1994 and issued the first proclamation that November. It is a national observance rather than a federal holiday.
memorial_us_pearl_harbor_remembrance_day.traditions: The American flag is flown at half-staff on federal buildings and at many homes until sunset. The principal ceremony is held at the Pearl Harbor National Memorial in Hawaii, near the USS Arizona Memorial, where survivors, veterans and families gather for a moment of silence marking the time the attack began, a rifle salute and the presentation of wreaths. Similar services take place at veterans' memorials across the country.
funFacts: The observance was created by Public Law 103-308, signed on 23 August 1994; the first official observance was 7 December 1994.
The USS Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor is built directly above the sunken hull of the battleship.
Pearl Harbor Remembrance Day is a national observance rather than a federal holiday, so offices and schools stay open.

memorial_za_human_rights_day.intro: Human Rights Day on 21 March commemorates the Sharpeville massacre of 1960 and celebrates the rights enshrined in South Africa's democratic constitution.
memorial_za_human_rights_day.history: On 21 March 1960 police opened fire on a peaceful crowd protesting the pass laws in Sharpeville, killing 69 people. The massacre drew worldwide condemnation of apartheid. After the first democratic elections the day was made a public holiday in 1994, and Nelson Mandela signed the new constitution in Sharpeville in 1996.
memorial_za_human_rights_day.traditions: Ceremonies are held at the Sharpeville memorial and Human Rights Precinct, and the government uses the day to promote the Bill of Rights. Communities organise marches, concerts and educational events.
funFacts: The United Nations declared 21 March the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination in 1966, in memory of Sharpeville.
The South African Bill of Rights is considered one of the most progressive in the world.
The Sharpeville memorial lists the names of all 69 victims on individual pillars.

memorial_za_youth_day.intro: Youth Day is a public holiday in South Africa, observed on 16 June. It remembers the Soweto uprising of 1976, when schoolchildren protesting against being taught in Afrikaans were met with police fire, and the many young people who died in the years that followed.
memorial_za_youth_day.history: A government decree required that several subjects in black schools be taught in Afrikaans alongside English, on top of the inferior schooling imposed by the Bantu Education Act. On the morning of 16 June 1976 thousands of pupils marched through Soweto in protest; police opened fire, and unrest spread to townships across the country and continued for months. A photograph of the dying Hector Pieterson, one of the first children shot, carried the story around the world. After the end of apartheid, 16 June became a public holiday in 1995.
memorial_za_youth_day.traditions: The president delivers a national address at a commemoration that moves between provinces each year, and wreaths are laid at the Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum in Orlando West, Soweto, close to where the shooting happened. Schools, youth organisations and municipalities hold marches, lectures and remembrance services, and the whole of June is observed as Youth Month, with programmes on education, work and the rights of young people.
funFacts: The whole of June is observed in South Africa as Youth Month.
The Hector Pieterson Memorial and Museum stands in Orlando West, near where the 1976 march was stopped.
The Organisation of African Unity declared 16 June the International Day of the African Child in 1991.

memorial_zw_heroes_day.intro: Heroes' Day in Zimbabwe is a public holiday on the second Monday of August. It honours those who died in the liberation struggle that led to independence in 1980, together with others later recognised as national heroes.
memorial_zw_heroes_day.history: Zimbabwe's independence in April 1980 followed a long armed struggle against white minority rule in Rhodesia, known in Zimbabwe as the Second Chimurenga. Fighters and civilians died in large numbers over more than a decade of conflict. After independence the new state set aside a day each August to remember them and built the National Heroes' Acre on a hillside outside Harare as the burial place for those granted national hero status. The holiday is immediately followed by Defence Forces Day on the second Tuesday of August.
memorial_zw_heroes_day.traditions: The main ceremony takes place at the National Heroes' Acre in Harare, where the president lays a wreath at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and addresses the nation. Provincial and district heroes' acres hold parallel ceremonies, families visit graves to lay flowers, and church services and veterans' gatherings are held. State broadcasters carry the Harare ceremony live, and a commemorative gala is often staged nearby.
funFacts: The National Heroes' Acre stands on a hillside a few kilometres from central Harare.
Heroes' Day is followed the next day by Defence Forces Day, giving two linked public holidays.
Burial at the National Heroes' Acre is reserved for those formally granted national hero status.

memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.intro: On 8 May, Europe remembers the end of the Second World War on the continent in 1945 and the millions of people who died in the war, in occupation and in the camps.
memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.history: The unconditional surrender of the German armed forces was signed in Reims on 7 May 1945 and again in Berlin-Karlshorst on 8 May, taking effect late that night. Many countries, among them France, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Ukraine, mark 8 May as a day of remembrance or a public holiday; in Germany it has been described as a day of liberation since a much-quoted speech by Federal President Richard von Weizsäcker in 1985. The United Nations designated 8 and 9 May as days of remembrance and reconciliation for those who lost their lives in the war.
memorial_eu_end_of_second_world_war_in_e.traditions: Wreath-laying ceremonies take place at war memorials, tombs of the unknown soldier and former concentration camps, often with a minute of silence and the reading of names. Veterans, officials and schoolchildren attend; flags fly at half-mast in some countries and at full mast in others that mark the day as a liberation. Survivors and their descendants share memories in schools and memorial sites.
funFacts: The surrender took effect at 23:01 Central European Time on 8 May 1945, which was already 9 May in Moscow.
The war in the Pacific continued until Japan surrendered in August and September 1945.
In Berlin the 8 May was a one-off public holiday in 2020, the 75th anniversary.
